Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 350 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2025)
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 350 is located in 
north-central Alberta, covering an area of 6224 km2. 
WMU 350 is bounded by Highway 33 to the west, The 
Athabasca River to the south and east, and the Lesser 
Slave Lake and River to the north (Fig. 1). The last 
population estimate of moose in this WMU was last 
completed in 2020 where the population had grown by 
58.8% since the previous 2015 survey, recovering 
towards historic high densities following a period 
between 2002 and 2015 during which the population 
had declined by 73%. 
F
igure 1. Wildlife Management Unit WMU350 in north 
central Alberta.  
Slave Lake and Nipisi woodland caribou 
population recovery  
WMU 350 includes a portion of the Slave Lake caribou 
population unit, along the western bank of the 
Athabasca River (Fig. 2). Annual wolf reductions were 
initiated in 2023 in response to declines in these 
caribou populations and have continued. While the 
declines in these caribou populations have slowed 
following wolf control, avoiding extirpation, the wolf 
control measures also reduce predation in deer and 
moose populations. This reduction in predation 
pressure on moose and deer can result in the growth 
of alternative prey populations to densities that can be 
counterproductive to caribou recovery objectives (i.e., 
apparent competition). Therefore, to address 
overabundant populations that could reduce the 
efficacy of predator reductions it is critical to monitor 
the response of moose and deer populations to inform 
potential management actions where predator control 
has reduced natural moose mortality. 
The objective of this survey was to update the 
population estimate, and population ratio for sex and 
age classes, for moose and to also record 
observations of other ungulates during the survey. An 
additional objective was to evaluate the response in 
ungulate populations to the caribou recovery 
management actions, and therefore, this survey was 
completed in a stratified design with WMU511 and 
adjacent WMUs to the northeast of WMU 350 to 
provide an estimate of moose population parameters 
for areas within and surrounding the Slave Lake 
caribou local population.

Survey Method 
The aerial survey for moose in WMU 350 was 
conducted between January 30 and February 6th, 
2025. Transects, up to 10 km in length and oriented 
north-south (Fig. 3), were established throughout the 
unit with 1.2 km spacing between transects.  
F
igure 3. Survey areas with randomly selected transects 
that were completed during the survey (orange) across 
Wildlife Management Units 350 and 511. 
Sampling design 
Transects were surveyed by selecting a random 
sample of these transects, iteratively by random seed 
each day. Each WMU was stratified into 2 broad 
landscape strata (low and high) based on an index of 
spring vegetation productivity and evaluating 
encounter rates for moose from historic datasets. The 
Enhanced Vegetation Index was used as a proxy for 
spring green-up approaching the calving period for 
moose. An aggregate dataset of annual mean EVI 
indices of the 16-day period ending on June 1, with 
500m resolution, was used to generate a relative index 
for the study area (Fig. 4). The Enhanced Vegetation 
Index are derived from normalized reflectance of red, 
near-infrared and blue spectrum from the MODIS 
system (NASA AppEARS) and provide a relative 
comparison of greenness of vegetation in the canopy 
(Didan et al., 2015). The initial sampling effort follows 
the random assignment of transects across the WMU, 
regardless of strata, but the efficacy of the additional 
strata  are used to iteratively evaluate the efficacy of 
changing the sampling intensity based on these strata 
if the sampling coverage across all strata were 
adequate (sufficient representation and coverage 
across all areas of the WMU), the precision would be 
improved, and survey costs would be decreased due 
to improved gains in precision.  
F
igure 4. The relative vegetation productivity across the 
survey areas is shown with annual spring Enhanced 
Vegetation Indices (EVI). A dataset of aggregated annual 
mean EVI indices for the 16-day period ending June 1, with 
500m resolution, was used to generate a relative index for 
the study area is displayed. Darker green areas represent 
higher productivity than lighter areas. The delineation 
between high and low strata is represented with a dashed 
line within WMUs 350 and 511. 
Survey method 
The distance sampling transect method (Buckland et 
al. 2001, Alberta Environment and Parks 2016) used

to estimate population density and abundance in the 
study area. Surveys are conducted with three 
observers in Bell 206 Helicopters with installed bubble 
windows. The rear observers are responsible for the 
detection of animals from the skid to the horizon, and 
the front left observer detects animals directly below 
the aircraft between the skids (e.g., the chin bubble of 
the BH206 configuration). Transects are surveyed with 
an approximate altitude between 100-150m above 
treeline, and at an airspeed between 90-110 km/h. 
When an animal is observed a waypoint on the 
transect and over the animal group are collected to 
calculate the perpendicular distance that is used to 
model the pattern of detection used to correct for the 
bias in the declining detection with distance from the 
aircraft. In addition to strata within WMU511, the 
concurrent survey of WMU350, immediately adjacent, 
with equivalent survey design and methods were used 
in the analysis to increase robustness of detection 
models.  
Ungulates were classified by age (adult or young) and 
sex (determined primarily by presence of a vulva 
patch). The category of moose activity (bedded, 
standing, bedded) and canopy cover, or vegetation 
cover within 10 m of the moose (0-33%, 43-66%, and 
>66%), were included as covariates to improve
estimates of detection probability and detection bias
associated with the survey. Although late winter
surveys occur after antler drop has occurred for many
individuals, the size of antlers were recorded for all
species, when present (Alberta Sustainable Resource
Development 2010).
While distance sampling estimates already account for 
the components of precision (i.e. detection probability 
except at g(0), encounter rate sampling variance, and 
group size variance), applying a bias correction (i.e. 
sightability bias correction), or estimating cohort-
specific abundance (i.e. cows, bulls, calves) requires 
an additional procedure to address the variation in bias 
correction models and composition ratio error 
estimates. Therefore, to address this additional 
uncertainty we used an integrated Monte Carlo 
modelling procedure to incorporate variance in the 
bias correction model and composition ratio estimates 
into abundance estimates across cohorts.  
Results 
A total of 1301km across 188 transect segments were 
sampled for a total of 30.7 hours of flight time, 
including deadhead. This effort corresponds to a 
survey coverage of 18.8% of the total area within the 
WMU (1171km2 of survey coverage). Survey 
conditions were considered excellent for most of the 
survey, although snow and extreme cold temperatures 
prohibited flights on some days during the survey 
period. Aircraft were equipped with specialized 
ventilation systems to reduce icing on the windows 
during transects. The iterative evaluation of the 
encounter rates and precision did not warrant 
differential sampling effort in the strata, however, 
estimates with and without the additional strata were 
included in the analysis.  
In total, 277 moose were observed on transects from 
209 independent group observations. A total of 277 
moose were classified of which 144 were cows, 62 
were calves and 71 were bulls. Of the bulls observed, 
80% had already shed their antlers at the time of the 
survey. Of those that still had antlers (n=14), 11 were 
considered small (small spike or forked antlers) and 3 
were medium (palmated, spread less than half the 
length of body). Thirty-eight percent of cows were 
observed with a calf at-side, and of those 7 cows had 
twins (13.0% twinning rate). One lone calf was 
observed during the survey. 
The bull:cow and calf:cow ratios were 0.471 (90% CI 
0.36-0.59) and 0.448 (90% CI 0.37 – 0.53), 
respectively. The prevalence of hair loss./rub typically 
associated with winter tick was low with only 6 
individuals (2.1%) with slight tick rub (<25% of total 
body surface). The density estimate was 0.417 moose/
km2 with a coefficient of variation (CV) of 9.0% (90% 
CI 0.36-0.48). The uncorrected estimated moose 
population for WMU 350 was 2593 (90% CI 
2207-2975). See Table 1 for a comparison to previous 
survey results using the relative uncorrected 
estimates. The mean density and abundance estimate 
corrected for detection bias (i.e., ‘sightability’) at g(0), 
was 2963 (90%CI 2592-3401)  moose with an 
estimated detection probability of 88.0% (90CI 
77-100%) across the entire survey. The moose 
population is estimated to have declined by 12.9% 
since the 2019/2020 survey, representing an annual 
average 
(geometric mean) population growth rate of 0.97 
although the confidence interval overlaps zero (90% CI 
0.93-1.02).

Most white-tailed deer had shed their antlers, and only 
4 adults were observed with antlers at the time of the 
survey (3 small and 1 medium). Therefore, adult deer 
could not be reliably assigned to sex classes and 
composition ratios were not calculated. In total, 372 
white-tailed deer were observed on transects from 163 
independent group observations. A total of 56 white-
tailed deer were classified of which 27 were antlerless 
adults, 24 were fawns and only 4 were classified as 
bucks.  
The fawn:antlerless adult ratio was 0.863 (90% CI 
0.71-1.02). The density estimate was 0.677 white-
tailed deer/km2 with a coefficient of variation (CV) of 
13.0% (90% CI 0.53-0.82). The uncorrected estimated 
white-tailed deer population for WMU 350 was 4212 
(90% CI 3309 - 5115). This is the first survey with 
sufficient observations to support an estimated 
population density for this WMU, and therefore 
comparisons to previous estimates are not possible 
(Table 3).
